metadata.description: Discover genetic conditions that can follow maternal mitochondrial or X-linked inheritance patterns, plus the family-history clues and testing steps worth knowing.
metadata.title: 20 Illnesses You Inherit From Your Mother

landing.title: 20 Illnesses You Inherit From Your Mother
landing.intro: Some can run in families for generations without anyone knowing.

icon.alt: Mother and adult daughter beside a glowing DNA helix

disclaimer: General educational information only. Inheriting a genetic variant does not always mean someone will develop a condition, and many of the conditions described can arise through more than one genetic mechanism. Family history and symptoms cannot confirm inheritance. A qualified clinician or genetics professional can provide individual advice and arrange appropriate testing.

sections.title: 20 Illnesses That Can Follow Maternal Inheritance Patterns
sections.intro: Mitochondrial DNA is generally inherited from the mother. The conditions below can follow that pattern when they are caused by a disease-associated mitochondrial DNA variant, but inheritance and severity can vary greatly.

points.title: MELAS
paragraphs: MELAS stands for mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes. It can involve seizures, severe headaches, muscle weakness, hearing loss and neurological episodes.
Many cases are linked to variants in mitochondrial DNA, particularly MT-TL1, and can therefore pass through the maternal line. The age of onset and severity can differ even among relatives.

points.title: MERRF
paragraphs: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers, or MERRF, can cause muscle jerks, seizures, poor coordination, muscle weakness and sometimes hearing or heart problems.
Common causes involve mitochondrial DNA variants such as changes in MT-TK. A mother carrying a disease-associated variant can pass it to sons or daughters, but their symptoms may not look identical.

points.title: Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy
paragraphs: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, or LHON, damages the optic nerve and can cause sudden or progressive loss of central vision, often beginning in adolescence or early adulthood.

LHON is commonly caused by mitochondrial DNA variants inherited from the mother. Not everyone who inherits a variant develops sight loss, showing why a genetic result is not always a prediction of symptoms.

points.title: Maternally Inherited Diabetes And Deafness
paragraphs: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness, often shortened to MIDD, combines diabetes with progressive hearing loss. Some people also develop eye, heart, kidney or muscle problems.

MIDD is most often associated with a mitochondrial DNA variant and may appear in several generations on the mother's side. Diabetes and hearing loss are common for many unrelated reasons, so the combination alone does not diagnose it.

points.title: NARP Syndrome
paragraphs: Neuropathy, ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa—NARP—can affect sensation, balance, coordination and vision. Learning difficulties, seizures or muscle weakness may also occur.

Some NARP cases are caused by variants in the mitochondrial MT-ATP6 gene. The proportion of altered mitochondrial DNA can influence whether a relative has mild symptoms, severe disease or no obvious symptoms.

points.title: Mitochondrial Leigh Syndrome
paragraphs: Leigh syndrome is a serious neurological disorder that often begins in infancy or childhood and can cause loss of movement skills, muscle weakness, swallowing problems and breathing difficulties.
Leigh syndrome has many genetic causes. Only the forms caused by mitochondrial DNA follow maternal inheritance; most other forms have different inheritance patterns.

points.title: Mitochondrial Nonsyndromic Hearing Loss
paragraphs: Certain mitochondrial DNA variants can cause hearing loss without the wider features of a mitochondrial syndrome. Hearing may decline gradually or become more vulnerable after particular antibiotic exposure.

Variants in genes such as MT-RNR1 can pass through the maternal line. Medication-related risk depends on the exact variant and circumstances, so treatment decisions need professional guidance rather than family assumptions.

points.title: Mitochondrial Complex I Deficiency
paragraphs: Complex I deficiency disrupts cellular energy production and can affect the brain, muscles, heart, liver or other organs. Its presentation ranges from severe childhood disease to later-onset symptoms.
It can result from either nuclear DNA or mitochondrial DNA variants. Maternal inheritance applies only when the responsible change is in mitochondrial DNA, which testing can distinguish.

points.title: Mitochondrial Complex III Deficiency
paragraphs: Complex III deficiency can cause muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, liver disease, neurological problems or a combination of features because cells struggle to produce energy efficiently.
Several genes can cause it and they do not all share the same inheritance pattern. A mitochondrial DNA cause may follow the maternal line, while a nuclear gene cause may not.

points.title: Mitochondrial Complex IV Deficiency
paragraphs: Complex IV deficiency, also called cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, can affect muscles, the nervous system, the heart and other high-energy tissues. Severity and age of onset vary widely.
Some forms are caused by mitochondrial DNA and can be maternally inherited; others come from nuclear genes inherited in different ways. The condition name alone does not reveal which pattern applies.

next.title: The Other 10 Can Pass Down A Different Way
next.copy: A mother's X chromosome can carry a completely different group of conditions—including several that often affect sons more severely.

sections.title: The Other 10 Conditions A Mother Can Pass On
sections.intro: A son receives his only X chromosome from his mother, while a daughter receives one X chromosome from each parent. That makes maternal transmission especially important in many X-linked conditions, although new variants and other family patterns can also occur.

points.title: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
paragraphs: Duchenne muscular dystrophy causes progressive muscle weakness, usually beginning in early childhood. It is caused by changes in the DMD gene on the X chromosome.
A mother carrying a disease-associated DMD variant can pass it to a son or daughter. Sons are more often severely affected, while some female carriers also develop muscle or heart symptoms.

points.title: Becker Muscular Dystrophy
paragraphs: Becker muscular dystrophy is also linked to the DMD gene but generally progresses more slowly and can begin later than Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
It follows an X-linked pattern. A carrier mother may pass the altered gene to either sex, and the exact variant helps explain why severity differs.

points.title: Hemophilia A
paragraphs: Hemophilia A reduces clotting factor VIII and can cause prolonged bleeding, easy bruising or bleeding into joints and muscles. Severity depends largely on remaining clotting-factor activity.
The F8 gene is on the X chromosome. A mother carrying an altered copy can pass it on, and some women and girls with the variant also have clinically important bleeding.

points.title: Hemophilia B
paragraphs: Hemophilia B affects clotting factor IX and can produce a bleeding pattern similar to hemophilia A. Laboratory testing distinguishes the two.
It is linked to the F9 gene on the X chromosome. Family history can be absent because a new variant may occur or previous carriers may not have been recognised.

points.title: Fragile X Syndrome
paragraphs: Fragile X syndrome can cause learning difficulties, developmental differences and characteristic behavioural or physical features. Males are often more significantly affected than females.

An FMR1 premutation can expand when passed through an egg, so maternal transmission is particularly important. Specialist interpretation is needed because premutations and full variants have different implications.

points.title: G6PD Deficiency
paragraphs: G6PD deficiency can make red blood cells break down after certain infections, foods or medicines, causing jaundice, dark urine, tiredness or anaemia.
The G6PD gene is X-linked. Males are often more clearly affected, but females can also have significant deficiency depending partly on X-chromosome inactivation.

points.title: X-Linked Adrenoleukodystrophy
paragraphs: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy can affect the brain, spinal cord and adrenal glands. Its forms range from childhood cerebral disease to adult spinal symptoms or adrenal insufficiency.
A mother with an ABCD1 variant can pass it to children. Women with the variant may also develop neurological symptoms later in life and should not automatically be described as unaffected carriers.

points.title: Fabry Disease
paragraphs: Fabry disease causes a fatty substance to build up in cells and may affect the kidneys, heart, nervous system, skin, hearing and risk of stroke.
It follows an X-linked pattern. Both males and females can have substantial medical problems, though symptoms and age of onset may differ within the same family.

points.title: Hunter Syndrome
paragraphs: Hunter syndrome, also called mucopolysaccharidosis type II, affects the body's ability to break down certain complex molecules. It can involve growth, joints, airways, hearing, the heart and development.
The IDS gene is on the X chromosome. It most often affects boys after transmission from a mother carrying the variant, although rare affected females and new variants are possible.

points.title: X-Linked Ichthyosis
paragraphs: X-linked ichthyosis causes dry, thickened or scaly skin, often becoming noticeable in infancy. Some people have additional features beyond the skin.
It usually results from a change or deletion involving the STS gene. A carrier mother can pass the altered X chromosome, with sons more commonly showing the classic skin condition.

next.copy: Maternal inheritance follows rules that can surprise families. One detail can change who is affected, how severely and whether the pattern is visible at all.

sections.title: Why Maternal Inheritance Can Be So Difficult To Spot
sections.intro: The phrase “inherited from your mother” hides several very different genetic mechanisms. Understanding which mechanism is involved is essential before estimating anybody's risk.

points.title: Mitochondrial DNA usually comes from the egg
paragraphs: The embryo generally receives its mitochondria—and therefore mitochondrial DNA—from the egg. This is why disease-associated mitochondrial DNA variants follow the maternal line rather than the paternal line.

points.title: A mother can carry mixed mitochondrial DNA
paragraphs: Cells can contain a mixture of altered and unaltered mitochondrial DNA, known as heteroplasmy. The proportions can differ between tissues and between relatives, affecting whether symptoms appear and how severe they become.

points.title: The same family can show very different symptoms
paragraphs: One relative may mainly have hearing loss while another has diabetes, muscle problems or neurological symptoms. Variable expression is one reason a maternal pattern may be missed for years.

points.title: A son receives his X chromosome from his mother
paragraphs: A son receives a Y chromosome from his father and an X chromosome from his mother. An altered X-linked gene from the mother therefore has no second X copy to offset it in a son.

points.title: Daughters can inherit X-linked variants too
paragraphs: A daughter receives one X chromosome from each parent. Depending on the condition and X-chromosome inactivation, she may have no symptoms, mild symptoms or significant disease.

points.title: Fathers and mothers do not pass X-linked variants in the same pattern
paragraphs: A father does not pass his X chromosome to sons, but he passes it to all daughters. A mother passes one of her two X chromosomes to each child, so each pregnancy is a separate event.

points.title: A new variant can appear without family history
paragraphs: Some genetic conditions result from a variant that arose for the first time in an egg, sperm or early embryo. No visible pattern in earlier generations therefore does not rule out a genetic cause.

points.title: Not every mitochondrial disease is maternally inherited
paragraphs: Mitochondria depend on genes in both mitochondrial DNA and nuclear DNA. Conditions caused by nuclear genes can follow autosomal or X-linked patterns instead, even when the diagnosis includes the word mitochondrial.

next.title: The Pattern Doctors Look For Isn't Always Obvious
next.copy: Who was affected, which side of the family they came from and how young they were can matter more than a single diagnosis.

sections.title: 8 Family-History Clues Worth Writing Down
sections.intro: A family history cannot diagnose a genetic condition, but a clear record can help a clinician decide whether specialist assessment or testing is appropriate.

points.title: The same unusual condition in several maternal relatives
paragraphs: Repeated diagnoses among a mother, her siblings, her mother or her mother's relatives may suggest a maternal pattern, especially for a confirmed mitochondrial DNA condition.

points.title: Related symptoms rather than identical diagnoses
paragraphs: Hearing loss, diabetes, muscle weakness, seizures, heart disease and vision problems may look unrelated until a clinician sees how they cluster across one side of a family.

points.title: Several affected boys connected through women
paragraphs: An X-linked pattern may show up as affected sons, brothers, maternal uncles or male cousins connected through female relatives. Women in the family may have milder or overlooked symptoms.

points.title: Symptoms appearing unusually young
paragraphs: The age when a condition began can be as informative as the condition itself. Record approximate ages at diagnosis, major symptoms and whether disease progressed.

points.title: Different severity within one family
paragraphs: A severe diagnosis in one relative and a mild version in another does not automatically rule out a shared genetic cause. Variable expression is common in several mitochondrial and X-linked conditions.

points.title: Known genetic test reports
paragraphs: The exact gene and variant listed on a relative's laboratory report can be far more useful than remembering that a test was “positive.” Ask permission before sharing another person's medical information.

points.title: Early deaths or unexplained diagnoses
paragraphs: Older records may use broad terms such as muscle disease, unexplained heart failure or childhood neurological illness. These details can sometimes help a genetics professional interpret the wider pattern.

points.title: Both sides of the family still matter
paragraphs: Do not collect only the mother's history. Most inherited and complex conditions involve genes from either parent, and shared habits or environments can also make illnesses cluster in families.

next.eyebrow: A FAMILY PATTERN IS NOT A DIAGNOSIS
next.title: Would A DNA Test Actually Give You An Answer?
next.copy: The right test may be very specific—or much broader—but testing without the correct context can create more questions than answers.

sections.title: What Genetic Testing Can—and Cannot—Tell You
sections.intro: Genetic testing is most useful when it begins with a careful personal and family history. The test selected, the person tested first and the way results are interpreted can all change what is learned.

points.title: Genetic counseling usually comes before the decision
paragraphs: A genetics professional can review diagnoses, symptoms and relatives on both sides of the family. They can explain whether testing is likely to help and what different results could mean.

points.title: Testing an affected relative can be more informative
paragraphs: When possible, testing may begin with someone who has the clearest confirmed diagnosis. Finding a specific variant can make targeted testing in relatives much easier to interpret.

points.title: Mitochondrial testing may need specialist interpretation
paragraphs: The amount of a mitochondrial DNA variant can differ between blood and other tissues. A negative blood result does not answer every possible mitochondrial question, so the clinical context matters.

points.title: A positive result does not always predict illness
paragraphs: Some variants have reduced penetrance, meaning not everyone who inherits them develops the condition. Results may also be unable to predict the age of onset or severity.

points.title: A negative result may not close the case
paragraphs: A test can miss a genetic cause if the responsible gene was not included, current technology cannot detect the change or the suspected diagnosis was incorrect.

points.title: An uncertain result is not a diagnosis
paragraphs: A variant of uncertain significance means there is not enough evidence to call a change harmful or harmless. It should not usually be treated as proof that a person has inherited a disease.

points.title: Results can have implications for relatives
paragraphs: A confirmed inherited variant may matter to siblings, children and other relatives. Genetic counseling can help plan respectful communication and identify who might benefit from testing.

points.title: Screening and treatment depend on the exact condition
paragraphs: Some results lead to regular heart, hearing, vision, metabolic or neurological checks; others may affect medicine choices or family planning. There is no single follow-up plan for “maternal inheritance.”

conclusion.copy: A condition appearing on your mother's side does not prove you inherited it, and an inherited variant does not always mean illness will develop. Record the family history you know and discuss concerning patterns with a qualified clinician or genetics professional before drawing conclusions or ordering a test.
